case_name: Johnson V.U. v State of Kerala

                IN THE HIGH COURT OF KERALA AT ERNAKULAM

              THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE P.V.KUNHIKRISHNAN

THIS       CRIMINAL   MISC.   CASE    HAVING   BEEN   FINALLY   HEARD   ON
07.08.2024, THE COURT ON THE SAME DAY PASSED THE FOLLOWING:
                                                      2024:KER:60051
Crl.M.C.6262/2016                 2



                 P. V. KUNHIKRISHNAN, J.
              -------------------------------------------
                     Crl.M.C.No.6262 of 2016
              -------------------------------------------
              Dated this the 7th day of August, 2024

                              ORDER

The petitioner is the sole accused in Crime No.649/2016

of Manantoddy Police Station.         The above case was originally

registered alleging offences punishable under Sections 153 and

153A(1) of the Indian Penal Code.

2.        On 07.09.2016, the 2nd respondent/defacto

complainant filed a complaint before the Circle Inspector,

Mananthavady alleging that, some members in the whatsapp

group of the revenue staffs in which petitioner is the Admin posted

some comments against the Chief Minister and his stand against

celebrating Onam during duty time. The complaint against the

petitioner is that the petitioner who is said to be Administrator

(Admin) of the whatsapp group of the revenue staffs is spreading

enmity between different groups on the grounds of religion and

with the sole intention of defacing the Chief Minister of the State of
                                                       2024:KER:60051
Crl.M.C.6262/2016                 3

Kerala and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony of

the community at large. Annexure-A1 is the complaint. According

to the petitioner, he is neither the Administrator nor in any way

connected with the whatsapp group of the revenue staff. It is

submitted that the 2nd respondent defacto complainant, who is not

in good terms with the petitioner, was waiting to trap the

petitioner with an ulterior motive and since the petitioner is a

Government employee, the 2nd respondent defacto complainant

initiated a false criminal case against him to remove him from the

service. Based on the complaint, Annexure-A2 FIR was registered

by the Manantoddy Police Station. According to the petitioner,

even if the entire allegations in Annexures-A1 and A2 are accepted,

no offence is made out. Hence this Criminal Miscellaneous Case.

3.        Heard counsel for the petitioner and the Public

Prosecutor.

4.        When this Criminal Miscellaneous Case came up

for consideration on 06.08.2020, this Court passed the following

order:

'I heard the learned counsel for the petitioner
         and learned Public Prosecutor in this matter. After
         having heard both sides, I am of the opinion that it is
                                                        2024:KER:60051
Crl.M.C.6262/2016                 4

        only just and reasonable that the matter is investigated
        and the outcome of investigation is reported to this
        Court. It is submitted on behalf of the State that Section
        153A of IPC stands already deleted and the investigation
        survives only as regards the alleged commission of
        offence punishable under Section 153 of IPC. It was
        further submitted by the learned Public Prosecutor that
        the investigation could be completed at the earliest point
        of time. I hope that the investigation could be completed
        within a month. It is directed that the final report shall,
        however, be submitted only after taking instruction from
        this Court.

Post on 08.09.2020.'

5.        From the above, it is clear that, what remains is

only Section 153 IPC. Section 153 IPC reads like this:

'153. Wantonly giving provocation with
         intent to cause riot--if rioting be committed; if not
         committed.--Whoever malignantly, or wantonly by
         doing anything which is illegal, gives provocation to
         any person intending or knowing it to be likely that
         such provocation will cause the offence of rioting to be
         committed, shall, if the offence of rioting be committed
         in consequence of such provocation, be punished with
         imprisonment of either description for a term which
         may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both; and
         if the offence of rioting be not committed, with
         imprisonment of either description for a term which
         may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.'

6.        This Court in Sanjeev S v. State of Kerala

[2023(3) KHC 324] considered the ingredients to attract the

offence under Section 153 IPC. It will be better to extract the
                                                         2024:KER:60051
Crl.M.C.6262/2016                  5

relevant portion of the above judgment.

'6. The essential ingredients to constitute the offence
         under Section 153 IPC are as follows :-

1. The accused did an illegal act.

2. The act was done malignantly or wantonly.

3. The act was done with the intention to
                      provoke or knowing that it will provoke a
                      person to cause the offence of rioting.

7. The word malignantly and wantonly are not used
         synonymously in the Section. The word malignantly is
         used for the purpose of expressing a higher degree of
         intensity or illwill. While the word wantonly means
         causing harm or damage deliberately. The Oxford
         Advanced Learners Dictionary defines the word
         malignantly as "having or showing a strong desire to
         harm somebody." Similarly, the word wantonly is
         explained as "in a way that causes harm or damage
         deliberately and for no acceptable reason."

8. Both these terms convey that the two expressions
         'malignantly' or 'wantonly' used in Sections 153 IPC
         indicate that there must be a higher degree of malice or
         evil that is projected or evident in the act alleged. The
         provision further requires that the act alleged to be
         done must be illegal. The word illegal is defined in
         Section 43 of IPC to mean everything which is an
         offence or which is prohibited by law, or which
         furnishes a ground for a civil action. As held in
         R.Venkatkrishnan v. Central Bureau of Investigation
         [(2009) 11 SCC 737], the word has to be given a wide
         meaning.

9. The prosecution allegation is that the word 'വട' when
         modified as 'വട' used by the accused has a tendency to
         defame the deceased in front of the public. If the act
         done by the accused is not ex facie illegal, however
                                                               2024:KER:60051
Crl.M.C.6262/2016                     6

         wanton or deplorable or undesirable or done with
         malice, unless the act by itself is an offence, it cannot
         be held to satisfy the penal provisions of Section 153
         IPC. The word 'വട' is not a defamatory term and the
         use of the said term in the context cannot be said to be
         defamatory. The word 'വട' in the Malayalam language
         merely refers to a food article and cannot be termed as
         a defaming word even in combination with other
         words. Therefore the act alleged cannot be termed to be
         illegal.

10. Further, to bring home the guilt of the offence
         under Section 153 IPC, it is necessary that the act gives
         provocation to a person and also provoke or is likely to
         provoke a rioting. Though, for the offence to be
         attracted, actual rioting need not occur.

7.         This Court in Rohit Krishna v. State of

Kerala [2023(6) KHC 249] again considered the ingredients of

Section 153 IPC. It will be better to extract the relevant portion of

this judgment herebelow:

'9. The prosecution case is that on 10.10.2015, the accused
        affixed a poster containing the picture of a lotus on an
        electric post using gum and while doing so the accused made
        commotion near Annamkulangara Devi Temple. I fail to
        understand how Section 153 IPC is attracted in the facts,
        even if the above allegations are accepted. The only overt act
        attributed to the accused is that he affixed a poster of a lotus,
        which is a symbol of a political party, on an electric post and
        made commotion. I am of the considered opinion that even if
        that act is accepted in toto, the offence under Section 153
        IPC is not made out. Of course, it may be an illegal act
        to affix a poster on an electric post. But affixing a
                                                         2024:KER:60051
Crl.M.C.6262/2016                  7

        poster containing the symbol of a recognized political
        party on an electric post cannot be treated as an act
        done malignantly or wantonly. In Sanjeev's case
        (supra), this court observed that the word malignantly
        and wantonly are not used synonymously in the
        section. The word malignantly is used for the purpose
        of expressing a higher degree of intensity or ill-will.

While the word wantonly means causing harm or
        damage deliberately. The words malignantly or
        wantonly used in Section 153 IPC, indicate that there
        must be a degree of malice or evil that is projected or
        evident in the act alleged. As I observed earlier, even if
        the entire allegations are accepted, the offence under
        Section 153 IPC is not made out.'

8.        From the above dictum, it is clear that, if the

act done by the accused is not ex facie illegal, however wanton or

deplorable or undesirable or done with malice, it cannot be

held to satisfy the penal provisions of Section 153 IPC. In

this case, Annexure-A1 is the complaint based on which the First

Information Report registered.          It is stated that, petitioner

is the Admin of a whatsapp group in which the employees of

revenue are members. In that whatsapp group, a member posted a

post which according to the defacto complainant is with an

intention to spread enmity among the religion. This Court perused

the complaint along with the alleged posting. It is true that such a

posting ought to have been avoided by the person who
                                                    2024:KER:60051
Crl.M.C.6262/2016              8

posted the same. But, the question is whether the same attracts

the offence under Section 153 IPC. I am of the considered opinion

that the same would not attract Section 153 IPC.       Therefore,

considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the

considered opinion that further investigation in the crime can be

terminated.

Therefore, this Criminal Miscellaneous Case is allowed.

All further proceedings in Crime No.649/2016 of Manantoddy

Police Station are quashed.

Sd/-

P. V. KUNHIKRISHNAN
                                        JUDGE

notes: Fetched via indiankanoon_client.get_document() (live API), cleaned via ik_text_cleaner.clean_document(). Originally surfaced as a live Lane B match for the LOC/transit-remand test scenario (a deleted X/Twitter post) and confirmed by the user via the app's unverified-judgments panel; run through the full curation process afterward (finality-checked, read in full, verbatim-verified) before being added here -- confirming a judgment in the app only records it to related_judgments_approved.json (a separate, gitignored reuse cache), it does NOT add it to this corpus by itself. CORRECTION vs. the initial assumption when this case was first spotted: the case is about IPC Section 153 (BNS 192, 'wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot'), NOT Section 153A -- the order itself notes 153A was dropped from the charges in THIS case during investigation (a case-specific charge decision by the prosecution), not a general constitutional strike-down like IT Act Section 66A. The judgment also does not decide whether a WhatsApp/social-media group ADMIN can be held liable for a MEMBER's post -- that question was raised in the complaint but the case was resolved purely on Section 153's own ingredients not being met, so this is not cited for any admin-liability principle. See chunks/johnson_vu_v_state_of_kerala_chunks.json (chunk_method='curated_excerpt') for the 2 curated holdings: the Section 153 essential-ingredients test (quoting Sanjeev S v State of Kerala and Rohit Krishna v State of Kerala verbatim within this judgment, folded in rather than fetched separately), and the application -- a social-media post critical of a public figure, even if it 'ought to have been avoided,' does not by itself satisfy Section 153 unless the act is independently illegal, malignant/wanton, and tends to cause rioting.
